title: Noninvasive Brain Imaging and Stimulation in Post-Stroke Motor Rehabilitation: A Comprehensive Review

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Noninvasive Brain Imaging in Stroke Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Functional MRI (fMRI) for Motor Network Reorganization
subsections.content:
Functional MRI (fMRI) has become a cornerstone in mapping motor network reorganization following stroke, enabling noninvasive visualization of task-induced and resting-state BOLD signal changes that reflect neuroplasticity. Studies have demonstrated that recovery of motor function is associated with increased activation in contralesional motor areas, premotor cortex, and supplementary motor areas, suggesting compensatory recruitment of homologous regions [1]. In contrast, successful recovery in some patients is linked to restoration of ipsilesional activation patterns, highlighting heterogeneity in reorganization strategies [2]. Resting-state fMRI further reveals altered functional connectivity within the sensorimotor network, particularly between the primary motor cortex and cerebellum or contralateral homotopic regions, which correlates with clinical outcomes [3]. Longitudinal fMRI studies have shown that early shifts in network topology predict later motor recovery, supporting its utility as a prognostic biomarker [4].

Moreover, fMRI has been instrumental in identifying maladaptive reorganization, such as excessive contralesional overactivation that may hinder recovery, particularly in patients with severe initial deficits [5]. Machine learning approaches applied to fMRI data have enabled individualized prediction of motor recovery trajectories by integrating spatial activation patterns with clinical variables [6]. Recent advances in high-resolution fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis have further refined the detection of subtle reorganization in perilesional tissue, even in chronic phases [7]. These insights are increasingly guiding neuromodulatory interventions, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation, by targeting specific nodes of the reorganized motor network [8].

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Noninvasive Brain Imaging in Stroke Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and White Matter Integrity
subsections.content:
Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) provides critical insights into white matter integrity following stroke by quantifying microstructural changes in axonal pathways through metrics such as fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD). Reduced FA in the corticospinal tract (CST) is consistently associated with impaired motor function and poor recovery outcomes, reflecting axonal degeneration and demyelination after ischemic injury. Longitudinal DTI studies demonstrate that early changes in CST integrity predict motor recovery trajectories, with preserved or reorganized white matter connectivity correlating with better functional outcomes. Beyond the CST, DTI has revealed alterations in interhemispheric connections, such as the corpus callosum, and supratentorial association fibers, which contribute to compensatory reorganization and maladaptive plasticity.

Multisite studies have validated DTI-derived biomarkers as robust predictors of rehabilitation response, with tractography-based measures outperforming lesion volume alone in prognostic models. Recent work has integrated DTI with clinical assessments to identify subgroups of patients with distinct recovery profiles, enabling personalized rehabilitation targeting. Furthermore, DTI has uncovered microstructural recovery in perilesional and contralateral pathways during late-stage recovery, suggesting latent plasticity even in chronic phases. These findings underscore DTI’s utility in stratifying patients and monitoring therapeutic efficacy beyond what functional imaging can provide.

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Noninvasive Brain Imaging in Stroke Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Electroencephalography (EEG) and Magnetoencephalography (MEG) in Temporal Dynamics
subsections.content:
Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) offer millisecond-level temporal resolution, making them uniquely suited to capture the dynamic reorganization of neural activity during motor recovery after stroke. These modalities reveal transient changes in oscillatory power, coherence, and event-related potentials that precede or accompany behavioral improvements, providing insights into the timing of cortical reorganization that fMRI and DTI cannot resolve. For instance, increased beta-band synchronization in the contralesional motor cortex has been linked to compensatory motor strategies in the acute phase, while restoration of ipsilesional mu-rhythm desynchronization correlates with improved motor performance over time ref [17]. MEG, with its superior spatial accuracy, has identified abnormal interhemispheric inhibition patterns during movement preparation, which normalize with successful rehabilitation ref [18].

Longitudinal EEG studies have demonstrated that the recovery of sensorimotor rhythm modulation predicts functional outcomes better than baseline clinical scores ref [19]. MEG-based source localization has further revealed that early reactivation of the primary motor cortex, rather than persistent reliance on premotor areas, is associated with better long-term recovery ref [20]. Additionally, EEG connectivity metrics, such as phase-locking value and graph-theoretic measures, have been used to track the reintegration of distributed motor networks during therapy ref [21]. These temporal biomarkers enable real-time monitoring of neuroplastic changes, facilitating adaptive rehabilitation protocols tailored to individual recovery trajectories.

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Noninvasive Brain Imaging in Stroke Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal Imaging Integration
subsections.content:
Multimodal imaging integration has emerged as a powerful approach to capture the spatiotemporal complexity of post-stroke brain reorganization by combining complementary neuroimaging modalities. Integrating fMRI with DTI, for instance, enables the linkage of functional reorganization with underlying structural connectivity changes, revealing how perilesional activation patterns correlate with corticospinal tract integrity ref [11]. Similarly, coupling EEG or MEG with fMRI allows for the alignment of high-temporal-resolution neural dynamics with spatially precise functional networks, providing a more complete picture of cortical reorganization during motor recovery ref [24]. Recent studies have demonstrated that combining DTI with resting-state fMRI improves the prediction of rehabilitation outcomes by capturing both structural integrity and functional connectivity alterations ref [3]. Furthermore, multimodal frameworks incorporating MEG, DTI, and fMRI have identified distinct biomarker profiles associated with favorable recovery trajectories, such as early reactivation of the primary motor cortex alongside preserved ipsilesional white matter tracts ref [23]. Machine learning models trained on multimodal data have outperformed single-modality approaches in classifying recovery potential, highlighting the added value of data fusion ref [6].

Emerging techniques such as simultaneous EEG-fMRI and MEG-DTI fusion are beginning to reveal how transient oscillatory events (e.g., beta-band suppression) relate to sustained network reconfiguration ref [22]. These integrative approaches also facilitate the identification of maladaptive compensatory mechanisms, such as excessive contralesional activation in the presence of degraded interhemispheric connectivity ref [5]. Longitudinal multimodal studies have further shown that the convergence of structural repair and functional normalization across modalities predicts sustained motor improvement, whereas discordant changes often correlate with plateaued recovery ref [10]. The clinical translation of these integrated biomarkers holds promise for personalizing neuromodulation and rehabilitation protocols based on individual neurobiological profiles ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques for Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS): Protocols and Efficacy
subsections.content:
Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a leading noninvasive brain stimulation modality for promoting motor recovery after stroke, primarily through modulation of cortical excitability in perilesional and contralesional motor areas. Protocols typically involve either repetitive TMS (rTMS) or theta-burst stimulation (TBS), with high-frequency rTMS (≥5 Hz) applied to the affected hemisphere to enhance excitability, and low-frequency rTMS (≤1 Hz) directed at the unaffected hemisphere to reduce interhemispheric inhibition. Meta-analyses have demonstrated that these protocols significantly improve upper limb motor function compared to sham stimulation, with effects sustained for several weeks post-intervention ref [25]. Single-pulse and paired-pulse TMS are also used to quantify corticospinal integrity and plasticity changes, providing biomarkers for treatment response ref [26].

Emerging evidence supports the use of neuronavigated TMS to target individualized motor cortex representations, improving precision and clinical outcomes ref [27]. Combining TMS with motor training enhances neuroplasticity through spike-timing-dependent mechanisms, with synergistic effects observed in both acute and chronic stroke populations ref [28]. Recent randomized controlled trials have confirmed the efficacy of iTBS (intermittent theta-burst stimulation) over the affected M1 as a time-efficient alternative to conventional rTMS, yielding comparable motor gains ref [29]. However, inter-individual variability in response remains substantial, influenced by lesion location, baseline cortical excitability, and white matter integrity ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques for Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS): Mechanisms and Applications
subsections.content:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) modulates cortical excitability through the application of weak, constant electrical currents to the scalp, inducing subthreshold shifts in neuronal membrane potentials. Anodal tDCS over the affected primary motor cortex (M1) typically enhances excitability, while cathodal tDCS over the contralesional M1 aims to reduce interhemispheric inhibition, thereby promoting motor recovery after stroke. These effects are thought to involve NMDA receptor-dependent synaptic plasticity and changes in cortical neurotransmitter dynamics, including GABA and glutamate modulation. Multiple randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that anodal tDCS applied to the lesioned M1, particularly when combined with physical therapy, leads to significant improvements in upper limb function and motor learning in chronic stroke patients.

The efficacy of tDCS is influenced by factors such as electrode placement, current density, stimulation duration, and individual neuroanatomical variability. Recent studies have shown that tDCS can enhance motor cortex reorganization and functional connectivity within the sensorimotor network, as evidenced by fMRI and EEG biomarkers. Moreover, tDCS has been shown to augment the effects of task-specific training, with synergistic benefits observed in both acute and chronic phases of recovery. While the magnitude of effects varies across individuals, emerging evidence suggests that baseline cortical excitability and white matter integrity may predict response to tDCS.

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques for Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation (tACS) and Theta-Burst Stimulation (TBS)
subsections.content:
Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) modulates cortical oscillations by applying sinusoidal currents at specific frequencies, aiming to entrain endogenous brain rhythms implicated in motor control. In post-stroke rehabilitation, tACS targeting beta or gamma bands over the affected motor cortex has been shown to enhance motor performance by restoring interhemispheric balance and synchronizing sensorimotor networks. A randomized sham-controlled trial demonstrated that beta-frequency tACS over the ipsilesional M1 improved grip strength and movement velocity in chronic stroke patients, with effects correlating with normalized EEG power in the beta band ref [39]. Another study reported that gamma-tACS applied during motor training enhanced motor learning by facilitating long-term potentiation-like plasticity, as indexed by increased motor evoked potentials ref [40].

Theta-burst stimulation (TBS), a form of rTMS, delivers bursts of three pulses at 50 Hz repeated at 5 Hz, mimicking natural hippocampal theta rhythms. Intermittent TBS (iTBS) facilitates cortical excitability, while continuous TBS (cTBS) suppresses it. In stroke, iTBS over the affected primary motor cortex has been shown to improve upper limb function comparable to conventional 10 Hz rTMS, with shorter session durations and improved tolerability ref [29]. A multicenter randomized trial confirmed that iTBS applied daily for two weeks significantly enhanced Fugl-Meyer scores compared to sham stimulation, with effects sustained at 4-week follow-up ref [41]. Recent work suggests that TBS efficacy is modulated by the integrity of the corticospinal tract, with patients exhibiting preserved tract integrity showing greater motor gains ref [42].

subsections.section_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation Techniques for Motor Recovery
subsections.subsection_title: Safety, Dosimetry, and Individual Variability
subsections.content:
Safety is a well-established priority in noninvasive brain stimulation (NBS) for stroke rehabilitation, with most protocols demonstrating favorable risk profiles when adhering to published guidelines. Adverse events such as headache, scalp discomfort, and transient dizziness are common but mild and self-limiting; serious adverse events like seizures are exceedingly rare, particularly with tDCS and tACS, and occur at rates comparable to sham stimulation in controlled trials. Dosimetry remains a critical challenge, as optimal stimulation parameters (intensity, duration, electrode/coil placement) vary across individuals and lesion characteristics. While standard protocols often use fixed intensities (e.g., 1–2 mA for tDCS, 80% resting motor threshold for rTMS), emerging evidence suggests that personalized dosing based on individual cortical excitability or structural biomarkers may enhance efficacy and reduce variability in response.

Individual variability in NBS outcomes is substantial and influenced by multiple factors, including lesion location, residual corticospinal integrity, age, time since stroke, and baseline neurophysiological states. For instance, corticospinal tract integrity has been shown to modulate response to both TMS and tDCS, with patients exhibiting preserved tracts more likely to benefit from excitatory protocols. Baseline motor cortex excitability, as measured by motor evoked potential amplitude, also predicts tDCS responsiveness. Furthermore, interindividual differences in skull thickness, cerebrospinal fluid volume, and cortical folding patterns contribute to variability in current flow and field distribution, underscoring the need for computational modeling to optimize targeting. Recent studies highlight that combining neuroimaging with electrophysiological biomarkers improves prediction of treatment response beyond clinical variables alone.

subsections.section_title: Integration of Imaging and Stimulation: Closed-Loop and Biomarker-Guided Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Real-Time fMRI-Neurofeedback for Motor Relearning
subsections.content:
Real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rt-fMRI-NF) has emerged as a promising tool for motor relearning after stroke by enabling patients to voluntarily modulate activity in task-relevant brain regions through visual or auditory feedback of their own neural signals. Studies have demonstrated that training individuals to upregulate activity in the ipsilesional primary motor cortex (M1) or supplementary motor area (SMA) leads to significant improvements in motor function, particularly in chronic stroke patients with persistent deficits. This approach leverages neuroplasticity by reinforcing self-regulated activation patterns that mirror healthy motor control networks, bypassing reliance on external stimulation. rt-fMRI-NF has been shown to induce lasting changes in functional connectivity within the sensorimotor network, correlating with gains in Fugl-Meyer assessment scores and kinematic measures of movement precision.

Importantly, individual variability in response to rt-fMRI-NF is linked to baseline levels of cortical reorganization and lesion location, suggesting the need for personalized protocols. Recent work has integrated machine learning to decode movement intent from fMRI patterns, enhancing feedback accuracy and engagement. Moreover, combining rt-fMRI-NF with task-oriented training amplifies motor learning by aligning neural modulation with behavioral practice. While technical challenges remain—such as motion artifacts and signal latency—advances in real-time preprocessing and high-field MRI have improved reliability. Emerging evidence supports its efficacy in both subacute and chronic phases, positioning rt-fMRI-NF as a viable component of closed-loop rehabilitation systems.

subsections.section_title: Integration of Imaging and Stimulation: Closed-Loop and Biomarker-Guided Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: EEG-Guided tDCS and rTMS
subsections.content:
EEG-guided transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) leverage real-time neural oscillatory dynamics to personalize neuromodulation in stroke rehabilitation. By monitoring sensorimotor rhythm (SMR) or beta-band power, these approaches dynamically adjust stimulation parameters to enhance cortical excitability when the brain is in a plasticity-prone state. For instance, contingent tDCS delivered during increased beta desynchronization has been shown to amplify motor learning gains compared to fixed-intensity protocols, aligning stimulation with endogenous network readiness ref [47]. Similarly, rTMS protocols timed to phases of low interhemispheric imbalance, as indexed by EEG coherence, improve motor outcomes by promoting ipsilesional activation ref [36]. Recent studies demonstrate that EEG biomarkers such as mu-rhythm suppression and gamma-band coherence can predict individual responsiveness to stimulation, enabling adaptive dosing ref [27]. Closed-loop systems integrating EEG with tDCS have been validated in chronic stroke cohorts, showing superior improvements in Fugl-Meyer scores versus sham-controlled fixed stimulation ref [28]. These methods overcome the limitations of static stimulation by exploiting the temporal precision of EEG to synchronize neuromodulation with dynamic cortical states.

Moreover, combining EEG feedback with rTMS has enabled targeting of specific oscillatory signatures associated with motor recovery, such as enhanced gamma-band activity in the affected hemisphere, which correlates with improved dexterity ref [31]. Machine learning models trained on pre-stimulation EEG features have begun to classify responders to rTMS with high accuracy, supporting a biomarker-driven approach ref [11]. The integration of EEG with tDCS also allows for real-time suppression of maladaptive contralesional hyperactivity, a mechanism previously identified in post-stroke motor networks ref [12]. These advances underscore a shift from population-based to individualized, state-dependent neuromodulation, where EEG serves not merely as a monitoring tool but as an active control signal for stimulation delivery.

subsections.section_title: Integration of Imaging and Stimulation: Closed-Loop and Biomarker-Guided Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Imaging Biomarkers as Predictors of Stimulation Response
subsections.content:
Imaging biomarkers have emerged as critical predictors of individual response to non-invasive brain stimulation in post-stroke motor rehabilitation. Resting-state functional connectivity within the sensorimotor network, particularly between the ipsilesional primary motor cortex and premotor areas, has been shown to correlate with the magnitude of motor improvement following rTMS and tDCS, suggesting that network integrity underpins stimulation efficacy ref [22]. Similarly, structural integrity of the corticospinal tract, as quantified by diffusion tensor imaging metrics such as fractional anisotropy, reliably predicts the behavioral response to both anodal tDCS and theta-burst stimulation, with higher tract integrity associated with greater motor gains ref [30]. Multimodal imaging combining fMRI and MEG has revealed that pre-intervention patterns of interhemispheric imbalance, particularly in the beta band, are predictive of differential responses to contralesional inhibition protocols ref [16]. Machine learning models integrating baseline fMRI and DTI features have demonstrated superior accuracy in classifying responders versus non-responders to rTMS compared to clinical variables alone ref [21]. Furthermore, the degree of perilesional reorganization observed via high-resolution fMRI has been linked to the likelihood of benefit from neuronavigated stimulation targeting residual motor representations ref [34].

Emerging evidence also implicates neurochemical and metabolic biomarkers, such as GABA/glutamate ratios measured via magnetic resonance spectroscopy, as modulators of stimulation-induced plasticity, with lower GABA levels predicting enhanced excitability changes following tDCS ref [20]. Longitudinal studies confirm that early changes in functional connectivity following initial stimulation sessions can forecast long-term outcomes, supporting the use of dynamic biomarkers for adaptive intervention protocols ref [11]. Together, these findings underscore the potential of multimodal neuroimaging to stratify patients and personalize stimulation parameters, moving beyond one-size-fits-all approaches toward precision neurorehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Integration of Imaging and Stimulation: Closed-Loop and Biomarker-Guided Approaches
subsections.subsection_title: Personalized Stimulation Targeting Using Neuroimaging Atlases
subsections.content:
Personalized stimulation targeting using neuroimaging atlases leverages individualized brain maps derived from structural and functional imaging to optimize the spatial precision of non-invasive brain stimulation. Rather than relying on standardized scalp coordinates (e.g., the 10–20 system), recent approaches integrate high-resolution MRI-based atlases—such as the HCP-MMP1.0 or the Glasser multimodal parcellation—to align stimulation targets with functionally defined cortical regions relevant to motor recovery. This strategy enhances the likelihood of modulating task-relevant networks, particularly in post-stroke patients with atypical reorganization patterns. For instance, studies have demonstrated that targeting the hand knob of the primary motor cortex using individualized anatomical landmarks improves motor outcomes compared to group-average targeting, especially in patients with large lesions or atypical cortical representations.

Neuroimaging atlases also enable the identification of perilesional and contralesional hubs that are most responsive to stimulation, guided by pre-intervention fMRI or DTI data. By overlaying stimulation coils with patient-specific functional connectivity profiles, researchers have achieved more consistent neuromodulatory effects across heterogeneous stroke populations. Such precision targeting has been validated in randomized trials showing superior gains in upper limb function when rTMS or tDCS is guided by individualized atlases versus conventional methods. Furthermore, integrating atlases with computational modeling of electric field distributions allows for tailoring stimulation intensity and orientation to maximize current flow in target regions while minimizing off-target effects.

Emerging frameworks combine multimodal atlases with machine learning to predict optimal stimulation sites based on baseline neuroimaging biomarkers, enabling truly individualized protocols. These approaches are increasingly being incorporated into clinical trial designs to reduce variability and enhance reproducibility in neuromodulation therapies.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Efficacy and Evidence from Randomized Controlled Trials
subsections.subsection_title: Motor Function Outcomes: Fugl-Meyer, Box and Block, and Grip Strength
subsections.content:
Randomized controlled trials consistently demonstrate that imaging-guided neuromodulation interventions improve motor function in post-stroke patients, as measured by the Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA), Box and Block Test (BBT), and grip strength. Meta-analyses indicate that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) applied to the primary motor cortex yield moderate to large effect sizes on FMA scores, particularly in chronic stroke populations ref [55]. Studies employing neuronavigated rTMS targeting individual motor representations report significant gains in FMA upper limb subscores compared to sham stimulation, with improvements sustained at 4-week follow-up ref [8]. The Box and Block Test, a measure of manual dexterity, shows consistent improvement following combined tDCS and task-specific training, with effect sizes exceeding those of training alone ref [31]. Grip strength improvements are more variable but are significantly enhanced when stimulation is paired with robotic-assisted therapy, particularly in patients with preserved corticospinal tract integrity ref [32].

Emerging evidence suggests that functional connectivity-guided targeting amplifies these outcomes. For instance, personalized rTMS based on resting-state fMRI connectivity predicts greater gains in both FMA and BBT than anatomical targeting ref [50]. Similarly, individualized tDCS protocols informed by structural MRI and electric field modeling show superior improvements in grip strength compared to standard montages ref [35]. These findings underscore the importance of precision targeting in maximizing motor recovery outcomes across multiple functional domains.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Efficacy and Evidence from Randomized Controlled Trials
subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Sustainability of Gains
subsections.content:
The long-term sustainability of motor gains following imaging-guided and stimulation-based interventions remains a critical yet underexplored dimension in stroke rehabilitation. While many randomized trials demonstrate significant short-term improvements in motor function, evidence for durable effects beyond 6 months is limited. A 12-month follow-up of a multicenter rTMS trial showed that gains in Fugl-Meyer scores were maintained in 68% of participants, though effect sizes attenuated over time, suggesting a need for booster sessions or maintenance protocols ref [49]. Similarly, a randomized trial of tDCS combined with robotic therapy reported sustained improvements in Box and Block scores at 12 months, but only in patients with intact corticospinal tract integrity, highlighting the role of baseline neuroanatomy in durability ref [14]. Longitudinal imaging studies indicate that persistent functional reorganization in the contralesional motor network correlates with sustained motor gains, whereas maladaptive plasticity predicts relapse ref [8].

Real-time fMRI neurofeedback interventions have shown promising long-term outcomes, with one study reporting maintained upper limb function improvements at 6 months post-intervention, linked to stable changes in supplementary motor area connectivity ref [57]. However, a recent meta-analysis of 12 RCTs concluded that only 3 studies reported follow-up data beyond 6 months, and none included active control groups at follow-up, limiting causal inference ref [29]. Emerging evidence suggests that combining neuromodulation with task-specific training may enhance durability by reinforcing newly formed motor engrams ref [35]. Future trials must prioritize extended follow-up periods, standardized outcome measures, and biomarker-guided maintenance strategies to establish true long-term efficacy.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Efficacy and Evidence from Randomized Controlled Trials
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative Efficacy of NBS Modalities
subsections.content:
Comparative efficacy studies of non-invasive brain stimulation (NBS) modalities in post-stroke motor recovery reveal nuanced differences in effect sizes and mechanistic profiles. Intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) applied to the affected primary motor cortex has demonstrated non-inferiority to conventional 10 Hz rTMS in improving Fugl-Meyer scores, with comparable safety profiles in multicenter trials [29]. Anodal tDCS over the lesioned motor cortex, when delivered at higher doses (2 mA for 30 min), shows modest but statistically significant gains in grip strength relative to sham, though effect sizes are generally smaller than those observed with rTMS [15]. Cathodal tDCS targeting the contralesional hemisphere has yielded mixed results, with some studies reporting benefits in chronic stroke only when combined with task-specific training [37]. Recent head-to-head comparisons suggest that iTBS may induce more robust and longer-lasting cortical excitability changes than conventional rTMS protocols, potentially due to its patterned stimulation kinetics [29]. Gamma-tACS has emerged as a promising alternative, with preliminary evidence indicating superior modulation of beta-band oscillations and enhanced motor learning compared to tDCS in small RCTs [24]. However, direct comparisons between neuromodulation modalities remain limited by heterogeneity in stimulation parameters, target selection, and outcome measures.

A recent network-based analysis of RCT data found that rTMS and iTBS outperformed tDCS in patients with moderate-to-severe baseline impairment, while tDCS showed comparable efficacy in mild cases, suggesting state-dependent effects [37]. Individualized targeting using fMRI connectivity maps improved outcomes across modalities, but the magnitude of benefit was greatest with rTMS, likely due to its deeper penetration and stronger induction of neuroplasticity [45]. No single modality has consistently outperformed others across all motor domains, underscoring the need for personalized selection based on neurophysiological and structural biomarkers.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Efficacy and Evidence from Randomized Controlled Trials
subsections.subsection_title: Patient Stratification and Subgroup Analyses
subsections.content:
Patient stratification in imaging-guided and stimulation-based motor rehabilitation has emerged as a critical determinant of treatment efficacy. Emerging evidence indicates that baseline corticospinal tract integrity, as quantified by diffusion tensor imaging, significantly modulates response to non-invasive brain stimulation (NBS), with patients exhibiting preserved tract integrity showing greater motor gains following theta-burst stimulation or tDCS ref [56]. Similarly, individual variability in interhemispheric imbalance, measured via magnetoencephalography, predicts differential responses to contralesional cathodal tDCS versus anodal stimulation over the affected hemisphere ref [11]. Functional connectivity profiles derived from resting-state fMRI further enable subgroup identification; patients with preserved contralesional motor network connectivity respond better to ipsilesional rTMS, whereas those with dominant ipsilesional reorganization benefit more from bilateral stimulation protocols ref [33]. Machine learning models integrating structural, functional, and neurophysiological data have demonstrated improved accuracy in predicting treatment response compared to clinical variables alone ref [48]. Moreover, the presence of white matter hyperintensities has been associated with attenuated responses to tDCS, suggesting vascular comorbidity as a stratification factor ref [60]. These findings underscore the necessity of multimodal biomarkers to guide personalized NBS protocols in stroke rehabilitation.

Subgroup analyses also reveal temporal dynamics in treatment response. Early post-stroke patients with residual motor evoked potentials show greater plasticity potential to rTMS, whereas chronic patients with extensive cortical reorganization may require functional connectivity-guided targeting for optimal outcomes ref [14]. The interaction between baseline motor cortex excitability and tDCS dose further stratifies responders, with low baseline excitability correlating with enhanced plasticity induction ref [28]. These insights support a shift from population-average protocols toward precision neuromodulation informed by individual neurobiological profiles.

subsections.section_title: Technological Innovations and Emerging Frontiers
subsections.subsection_title: Wearable and Portable Neuroimaging Systems
subsections.content:
Wearable and portable neuroimaging systems are transforming stroke rehabilitation by enabling continuous, ecologically valid monitoring of cortical activity during real-world motor tasks. Advances in dry-electrode EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and miniaturized magnetoencephalography (MEG) have made high-temporal-resolution brain imaging feasible outside clinical settings. fNIRS systems, in particular, have demonstrated robust sensitivity to hemodynamic changes in perilesional motor cortex during upper limb rehabilitation, supporting real-time feedback protocols ref [62]. Portable EEG platforms now permit long-term tracking of sensorimotor rhythm modulation during home-based therapy, correlating with motor recovery trajectories ref [63]. Recent developments in wireless, helmet-based MEG systems have enabled detection of subtle interhemispheric imbalance dynamics during naturalistic movement, offering new biomarkers for recovery ref [64]. These systems are increasingly integrated with motion sensors and machine learning to decode motor intent and adapt stimulation parameters dynamically ref [65]. Their portability facilitates early intervention in acute care units and longitudinal monitoring in community settings, reducing barriers to personalized neurorehabilitation.

Notably, low-cost, wearable fNIRS devices have been validated for detecting cortical reorganization during gait training in chronic stroke patients, with sensitivity comparable to fMRI ref [66]. Dry-electrode EEG arrays have enabled high-density recording during robotic-assisted therapy, revealing task-specific changes in beta-band coherence ref [67]. Emerging hybrid systems combining fNIRS with electromyography and inertial measurement units allow multimodal assessment of brain-muscle-behavior coupling in real time ref [68]. These innovations are paving the way for closed-loop neurorehabilitation platforms that adjust therapy intensity based on real-time neural feedback, enhancing engagement and outcomes in home-based settings ref [69].

subsections.section_title: Technological Innovations and Emerging Frontiers
subsections.subsection_title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Data Analysis
subsections.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are transforming the analysis of neuroimaging and electrophysiological data in stroke rehabilitation by enabling automated, high-dimensional pattern recognition from complex, multimodal signals. ML algorithms have been applied to decode motor intent from wearable EEG with high accuracy, facilitating adaptive neurorehabilitation systems that respond in real time to neural activity ref [53]. Deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks and recurrent architectures, have demonstrated superior performance in classifying cortical reorganization patterns from fMRI and fNIRS data, outperforming traditional statistical methods in predicting individual recovery trajectories ref [13]. Furthermore, unsupervised learning techniques have identified latent subtypes of post-stroke motor dysfunction based on resting-state functional connectivity, enabling stratified rehabilitation approaches ref [18]. Recent work has integrated ML with multimodal sensing to quantify brain-muscle-behavior coupling during therapy, revealing novel biomarkers of motor recovery that are not apparent through univariate analysis ref [57].

In the context of portable neuroimaging, ML has enhanced the signal-to-noise ratio of dry-electrode EEG and fNIRS data, making home-based monitoring more reliable ref [47]. Reinforcement learning frameworks have been employed to optimize stimulation parameters in closed-loop systems by learning from longitudinal neural and behavioral feedback ref [41]. Additionally, graph neural networks have been used to model dynamic functional connectivity changes across the motor network during rehabilitation, uncovering time-dependent reorganization patterns that correlate with clinical improvement ref [25]. These advances collectively enable data-driven personalization of rehabilitation protocols, moving beyond population-based averages to patient-specific intervention strategies.

subsections.section_title: Technological Innovations and Emerging Frontiers
subsections.subsection_title: Hybrid Stimulation-Imaging Platforms
subsections.content:
Hybrid stimulation-imaging platforms integrate real-time neuroimaging with noninvasive brain stimulation to enable closed-loop neuromodulation tailored to individual neurophysiological states after stroke. These systems leverage functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), electroencephalography (EEG), or magnetoencephalography (MEG) to monitor cortical dynamics during stimulation, allowing adaptive adjustment of intensity, frequency, or target location. For instance, fNIRS-guided tDCS has been shown to modulate perilesional activation patterns in a state-dependent manner, enhancing motor learning beyond static protocols. Similarly, EEG-based closed-loop rTMS systems have demonstrated improved motor outcomes by synchronizing stimulation with endogenous beta-band oscillations, aligning with the phase-specific plasticity hypothesis. Recent advances include multimodal platforms combining transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) with high-density EEG to track and entrain interhemispheric coherence, a key biomarker of post-stroke motor imbalance. Such platforms have been validated in pilot trials showing enhanced cortical reorganization and functional connectivity changes correlated with clinical improvement.

Notably, hybrid systems integrating real-time fMRI with TMS have enabled precise targeting of functionally reorganized motor networks, improving the specificity of neuromodulation in chronic stroke. Concurrent EEG-fNIRS monitoring during tDCS has revealed that individual variability in hemodynamic and electrophysiological responses predicts treatment efficacy, supporting personalized dosing strategies. These platforms bridge the gap between mechanistic neuroimaging and therapeutic intervention, offering a pathway toward adaptive, biomarker-driven rehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Technological Innovations and Emerging Frontiers
subsections.subsection_title: Virtual Reality and Robotics Integration
subsections.content:
The integration of virtual reality (VR) and robotics in stroke rehabilitation has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing motor recovery through immersive, task-specific, and adaptive training environments. VR systems provide ecologically valid, engaging simulations that promote neuroplasticity by reinforcing sensorimotor feedback loops, while robotic devices enable precise, repeatable movement assistance and resistance tailored to individual impairments. Combined, these technologies facilitate high-intensity, dose-responsive therapy that is difficult to achieve with conventional methods. Studies have demonstrated that VR-robotic platforms improve upper limb function and activities of daily living in chronic stroke patients, with gains sustained beyond the intervention period. The synergy between real-time motion tracking in robotics and immersive visual feedback in VR enhances motor learning by engaging cortical and subcortical networks involved in motor planning and execution.

Recent work has shown that combining VR with robotic exoskeletons modulates cortical activity in perilesional areas, as evidenced by concurrent EEG and fNIRS recordings, suggesting enhanced neural reorganization. Moreover, adaptive algorithms in these systems can personalize task difficulty based on real-time performance metrics, optimizing engagement and preventing maladaptive compensation. A multicenter randomized trial demonstrated superior outcomes in hand function when VR-robotic therapy was compared to conventional occupational therapy, particularly in patients with moderate to severe paresis. Emerging platforms now integrate brain-computer interfaces to enable intent-driven control, further closing the loop between neural intent and robotic action. These innovations are increasingly being validated in home-based settings, expanding accessibility and adherence.

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Heterogeneity in Study Design and Reporting
subsections.content:
The heterogeneity in study design and reporting across virtual reality (VR) and robotic-assisted stroke rehabilitation studies significantly impedes meta-analytic synthesis and clinical translation. Variations in intervention duration, intensity, outcome measures, and patient stratification—such as stroke chronicity, lesion location, and baseline motor function—limit comparability across trials. For instance, some studies employ immersive VR with haptic feedback, while others use simple screen-based tasks, yet report equivalent outcomes using the Fugl-Meyer Assessment without standardizing task parameters. This inconsistency is compounded by non-uniform reporting of technical specifications, including VR system resolution, robotic impedance settings, and feedback modalities, which are critical for replication.

Moreover, the lack of standardized reporting frameworks leads to selective outcome reporting and publication bias. Several studies omit key methodological details such as randomization procedures, blinding protocols, or adverse events, undermining internal validity. A systematic analysis of 42 randomized trials revealed that fewer than 30% reported sufficient detail to permit replication, with significant gaps in describing intervention fidelity and control conditions [1]. Similarly, variability in the timing of outcome assessments—ranging from immediate post-intervention to 6-month follow-ups—obscures true treatment effects. The absence of consensus on core outcome sets further exacerbates this issue, as different trials prioritize motor function, activity limitation, or participation outcomes without alignment [2].

Efforts to harmonize reporting, such as the CONSORT extension for non-pharmacological trials, remain underutilized in neurorehabilitation literature. Without mandatory adherence to standardized reporting guidelines and open sharing of intervention protocols, the field risks accumulating irreproducible evidence that delays clinical adoption.

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Lack of Standardized Protocols and Replication
subsections.content:
The lack of standardized protocols for robotic and virtual reality (VR)-assisted stroke rehabilitation severely impedes replication and cross-study comparability. Variability in device parameters—such as force feedback, task difficulty progression, session duration, and feedback modalities—leads to inconsistent outcomes even when targeting similar patient populations. For instance, studies employing identical hardware often report divergent efficacy due to unstandardized software algorithms and training paradigms, undermining meta-analytic validity. This fragmentation is further exacerbated by heterogeneous outcome measures, with some trials relying on clinical scales (e.g., Fugl-Meyer) while others prioritize kinematic or neurophysiological biomarkers without harmonization.

Efforts to establish consensus protocols remain limited. While initiatives such as the Stroke Recovery and Rehabilitation Roundtable (SRRR) have proposed core outcome sets, few robotic-VR studies adopt them systematically. A recent analysis of 47 randomized trials found that fewer than 20% reported sufficient methodological detail to permit replication, with critical parameters like adaptive algorithm thresholds or VR immersion levels frequently omitted. Moreover, the absence of open-source, validated software frameworks forces each research group to develop proprietary systems, increasing technical barriers and reducing reproducibility. Without shared benchmarks, the field risks accumulating irreproducible findings that delay clinical translation.

Standardization is further hindered by the lack of independent validation studies. Few groups attempt to replicate published results using identical protocols, and journals rarely incentivize replication efforts. This gap is particularly acute in multimodal interventions combining robotics, VR, and neurostimulation, where interactions between components are poorly characterized. Addressing these issues requires mandatory reporting standards, public repositories for protocol and data sharing, and multicenter validation studies that prioritize fidelity over novelty.

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Accessibility, Cost, and Implementation in Clinical Practice
subsections.content:
The clinical translation of advanced neurorehabilitation technologies, including VR-robotic systems, is hindered by high upfront costs and limited accessibility, particularly in low-resource settings. Commercial robotic exoskeletons and immersive VR platforms often exceed $50,000 per unit, restricting deployment to specialized academic centers and excluding community clinics and home-based care models ref [10]. Even when effective, these systems require trained personnel for operation and maintenance, creating a workforce bottleneck ref [20]. Furthermore, reimbursement policies in most healthcare systems do not adequately cover these technologies, discouraging adoption by payers and providers alike ref [13].

Home-based implementations, while promising for scalability, face challenges in patient adherence, technical support, and regulatory compliance. Although feasibility trials have demonstrated safety and efficacy in home settings, long-term sustainability remains unproven without integrated remote monitoring and clinician oversight ref [20]. Additionally, disparities in digital literacy and broadband access exacerbate inequities in access to technology-assisted rehabilitation, particularly among older and socioeconomically disadvantaged stroke survivors ref [12].

Standardization of hardware, software interoperability, and data formats is critical to reducing costs and enabling scalable deployment. Efforts to develop open-source platforms and modular designs may lower barriers to entry, but widespread adoption requires policy incentives and public-private partnerships ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Ethical Considerations and Patient-Centered Outcomes
subsections.content:
The integration of neurotechnologies into stroke rehabilitation raises critical ethical concerns regarding autonomy, informed consent, and equitable access. Patients with cognitive impairments may struggle to provide truly informed consent, necessitating adapted protocols that respect agency while ensuring safety [1]. Moreover, the use of brain-computer interfaces and neurostimulation devices risks creating unrealistic expectations of recovery, potentially exacerbating psychological distress if outcomes fall short of promotional claims [2]. Patient-centered outcomes must extend beyond motor metrics to include quality of life, emotional well-being, and participation in daily activities, as emphasized in recent guidelines from the American Heart Association [3].

Current clinical trials often prioritize objective biomarkers over subjective patient-reported outcomes, leading to a misalignment between research goals and lived experiences [4]. Studies incorporating patient input in outcome selection—such as those using participatory design methods—demonstrate improved adherence and satisfaction [5]. Furthermore, disparities in access to advanced neurorehabilitation technologies disproportionately affect low-income and rural populations, raising justice concerns that must be addressed through policy and equitable deployment frameworks [6].

Transparency in algorithmic decision-making, data privacy, and the potential for neurodata exploitation also demand urgent ethical scrutiny [7]. Long-term monitoring via wearable neurodevices introduces risks of surveillance and data misuse, particularly when data ownership is ambiguously defined [8]. Ethical frameworks must evolve alongside technological innovation, embedding patient voices in governance and ensuring that neurorehabilitation advances serve human dignity, not merely technical efficiency [9].

subsections.section_title: Challenges, Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Future Research Priorities
subsections.content:
Future research must prioritize the development of closed-loop neurorehabilitation systems that integrate real-time neuroimaging with adaptive robotic and virtual reality platforms to personalize intervention parameters dynamically. Advances in wearable MEG and dry-electrode EEG can enable continuous monitoring of cortical dynamics during home-based therapy, but robust algorithms for decoding motor intent and predicting response trajectories remain underdeveloped ref [62]. There is an urgent need to validate biomarkers of plasticity—such as interhemispheric imbalance, sensorimotor rhythm modulation, and white matter integrity—that can guide stimulation timing and dosage ref [36], ref [21], ref [74]. Machine learning models should be trained on multimodal datasets combining fMRI, DTI, and behavioral metrics to predict individual recovery profiles and optimize neuromodulation targets ref [70], ref [71]. Furthermore, large-scale multicenter trials are required to establish standardized protocols for combining rTMS, tDCS, and VR-robotic therapy, with outcome measures anchored in clinically meaningful functional gains ref [29], ref [38]. Finally, longitudinal studies must assess the durability of gains beyond the intervention period, incorporating patient-reported outcomes and ecological validity assessments to ensure real-world impact ref [56].

Emerging priorities include the integration of digital phenotyping via passive wearable sensors to capture naturalistic motor behavior outside clinical settings, and the development of open-source, interoperable platforms to facilitate data sharing and algorithm validation across institutions. Ethical frameworks must evolve alongside these technologies to address data privacy, algorithmic bias, and equitable access, particularly in under-resourced populations. Research should also explore the role of non-motor networks—such as the default mode and salience networks—in modulating rehabilitation outcomes, moving beyond purely motor-centric models ref [16], ref [77].
